analysis.one_liner: Strips health insurers' exemption from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote after being referred to the House Judiciary Committee in February 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, the McCarran-Ferguson Act has exempted the insurance industry from most federal antitrust laws, the statutes that make it illegal for companies to fix prices, divide markets, or block competitors. This bill would carve health insurance out of that exemption, so health insurers would be subject to the same antitrust rules as other industries. It also applies the ban on unfair methods of competition to nonprofit insurers, not just for-profit ones. The bill never received a committee vote or a hearing in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and employers who buy health insurance. Allowing federal antitrust enforcement against health insurers could break up or deter price-fixing, market division, and other anticompetitive conduct in a market where a few insurers dominate many states and regions, which could lower premiums and improve plan options [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurance customers and small employers

how_it_helps.text: Amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act so that nothing in it shields the business of health insurance from any of the federal antitrust laws, restoring the ability of the Justice Department and private plaintiffs to challenge anticompetitive conduct by health insurers [S2][S3].

Applies the Federal Trade Commission Act's prohibition on unfair methods of competition to health insurance regardless of whether the insurer is for-profit or nonprofit, closing a gap in the FTC's jurisdiction over nonprofit insurers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, which would lose the legal immunity they have held under the McCarran-Ferguson Act since 1945 and face antitrust scrutiny and potential lawsuits like other industries [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill does not itself lower premiums or require insurers to merge or divest anything; it only restores the possibility of antitrust enforcement, so its practical benefit depends on regulators and courts actually bringing cases against concentrated insurers.

Supporters of the McCarran-Ferguson exemption have argued that state insurance regulators already police the industry and that full antitrust exposure could reduce information-sharing among insurers, such as pooled claims data, that some argue helps smaller insurers price coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a specific, well-documented competitive problem: a handful of insurers control large shares of many local health insurance markets, and they have operated under a federal antitrust exemption since 1945. The cost of the bill fell almost entirely on insurers through legal exposure, and its main limit is that it creates enforcement authority rather than guaranteed results. On balance, restoring standard antitrust rules to one of the most concentrated parts of the economy was a modest, targeted change with real potential upside for consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its antitrust subcommittee, where it stayed until Congress ended in January 2015 without a hearing, vote, or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio, joined by Rep. Louise Slaughter, introduced the Health Insurance Industry Fair Competition Act on February 15, 2013 [S3][S1].

The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, and on April 8, 2013 it was sent to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law, where it remained with no further action recorded [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill never received a committee vote, a hearing recorded in the action history, or a floor vote, so it expired [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept the federal antitrust exemption they have held under the McCarran-Ferguson Act since 1945, insulating them from federal antitrust enforcement for the rest of the 113th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, whose antitrust exemption survived

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore federal antitrust law to the business of health insurance.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote after referral; the bill moved to a subcommittee and died there.

against.name: Chair, House Judiciary Committee (Rep. Bob Goodlatte)
against.role: Committee chairman who sets the markup calendar
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule the bill for committee action during the two years it sat in the committee's jurisdiction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsorship in a Republican-controlled House, and it received no action in the Republican-led Judiciary Committee; no Republican cosponsor is listed [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would end health insurers' special exemption from federal antitrust laws under McCarran-Ferguson, exposing pricing, market-division, and merger conduct to federal enforcement. Insurers benefit from that exemption, and their interest in keeping it runs against consumers who face premiums set in concentrated markets [S2][S3].
